title: Record Sargassum Surge Smothers Caribbean Beaches as Mexico Scrambles to Protect Tourism
excerpt: Mexico has cleared over 105,000 metric tons of seaweed this year — already surpassing 2025's record — as NASA data shows the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt near all-time highs.
body:
• Mexico has collected over 105,000 metric tons of sargassum from its Caribbean beaches in 2026, already surpassing last year's record of 92,783 tons with the season running through October.
  • NASA's PACE satellite ranked 2026 as the second-highest sargassum year ever recorded, with the Gulf of Mexico seeing nearly double its previous record at 5 million metric tons in June alone.
  • Scientists say the 2025 bloom was so massive it never fully dissipated, seeding an early 2026 regrowth now fueled by agricultural runoff and warming seas.
  • Mexico plans to invest $115 million in seaweed removal, but cleanup crews can only handle 1,200 of the 9,000 tons reaching shores on peak days.

Mexico is fighting a losing battle against a record deluge of sargassum, the foul-smelling brown seaweed now blanketing beaches across the Caribbean coast and threatening the country's multibillion-dollar tourism industry.

Officials in Quintana Roo — home to Cancun, Playa del Carmen, and Tulum — have cleared more than 105,000 metric tons of sargassum so far this year, according to state data released in mid-August. That figure already exceeds the full-year record of 92,783 tons set in 2025 and puts the state on pace to blow past earlier projections of 119,000 tons for the year, Reuters reported.

A Belt That Stretches 5,500 Miles

The problem is not confined to Mexico. NASA's PACE satellite and the University of South Florida's Optical Oceanography Laboratory have been tracking the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt, a sprawling mass of floating algae stretching roughly 5,500 miles from West Africa to the Americas. In June, the belt's abundance made 2026 the second-highest sargassum year in the satellite record, trailing only 2025.

The Gulf of Mexico bore the worst of it. Sargassum levels there nearly doubled the previous record, reaching 5 million metric tons in June alone, while the Caribbean Sea also hit all-time highs. Across the Atlantic, Caribbean, and Gulf, researchers measured some 27 million metric tons in July, according to the Associated Press.

"None of this is normal. Every year is a little bit of a new story."

— Brian Barnes, Marine Scientist, University of South Florida

Why It Keeps Getting Worse

Scientists say the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt has been growing since 2011, when it first appeared. Before that year, there was essentially nothing. Since then, the total sargassum mass has more than doubled every five years, according to USF optical oceanographer Chuanmin Hu.

The 2025 bloom — the largest ever at 40 million metric tons — was so massive it never fully dissipated. "The 2025 bloom was so big it never really left," Barnes told the AP. "It was enough to start a new bloom locally." For the first time, scientists have observed sargassum reproducing in large quantities within the Caribbean and Gulf itself, rather than being swept in by ocean currents from the central Atlantic.

Nutrient-rich agricultural runoff — particularly fertilizer-linked nitrogen and phosphorus from Brazil — along with warming seas and shifting ocean currents are fueling the outsized blooms. As sargassum decomposes on beaches, it releases hydrogen sulfide gas, producing a rotten-egg smell that irritates airways and drives tourists away.

Tourism Under Siege

"The drop in tourism is extremely serious," Tulum Councilman Eugenio Barbachano told Reuters. "The low season is not just low, it is critical."

Quintana Roo's governor, Mara Lezama, said the state plans to invest $115 million to combat the seaweed. But the scale of the challenge is daunting. On peak days, up to 9,000 tons of sargassum reach Mexico's Caribbean coastline — yet current resources can remove only 1,200 tons daily. Workers on the ground describe the task as relentless.

"This year it didn't stop. From July to July, sargassum kept arriving. It's basically impossible to keep it under control this year."

— Vitinia Villamontes, Cleanup Worker, Puerto Morelos

Some companies are trying to turn the crisis into an opportunity. Carbonwave, which processes sargassum into liquid biostimulants and fertilizers, argues that creating commercial value from the algae could offset removal costs. Mexico's environment ministry has identified dozens of potential uses, including biofuels and bioplastics, but public funding remains focused on cleanup.

What Travelers Should Know

The sargassum season could last until early or mid-October, according to Quintana Roo's environment minister Oscar Rebora, though conditions vary dramatically between beaches only a few miles apart. Tools like the USF Sargassum Watch System and NOAA's weekly Sargassum Inundation Risk forecast offer daily estimates that can help travelers gauge conditions before booking.

Resorts across the Riviera Maya have deployed containment barriers and collection boats, with many maintaining dedicated cleanup crews. Travelers planning Caribbean or Mexico beach trips this fall should contact their resort directly to confirm removal efforts and consider north- or west-facing beaches, which typically see less accumulation.
